This study examines the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks applied to determining the ground state of the Schr\"odinger operator within a $d$-dimensional hypercube framework. Under the assumption that the ground state resides in a spectral Barron space, the authors establish that the convergence of the generalization error remains decaying at a rate unaffected by dimensionality $d$. They support this assumption by introducing and validating a novel regularity condition for the ground state in terms of spectral Barron spaces. This derivation relies on constructing a fixed-point argument derived from the Krein-Rutman theorem.

This study analyzes the spatial and temporal evolution of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays recorded over an eight-year period by the Pierre Auger Observatory, focusing on events exceeding 8 EeV. Our findings reveal evidence for long-term modulation, potentially influenced by seasonal variations, although statistical significance is currently limited. While most observations align with expectations under isotropic conditions, a notable exception exists around the southern horizon. In contrast to previous investigations utilizing a template-fitting methodology, we employ the Oscillating Plane technique to examine these uhcrr; consequently, our conclusions regarding cosmic-ray anisotropies differ. Specifically, our analysis indicates no evidence for any directional preference in cosmic rays above 8 EeV.

This paper details and evaluates a endod- to-end solution for creating histopathology image analysis models using federated learning (FL). The methodology employs an federated segmentation framework where neural networks process local datasets within client institutions, ensuring data remains private on-site before sharing only model updates centrally for aggregation. The refined approach incorporates strategies to manage diverse network architectures, compensate for non-identifiable, stochastic optimization at both clients and servers, address varying data distributions across sites, tolerates data missing from certain clients, minimizes communication rounds by double folding model uploads, and utilizes compression for optimized performance. Performance metrics are tested against a federal collection comprising 72,000 images from five universities, comparing the system to both centralized segments involving all data and local modeling executed separately at each institution. The findings demonstrate that the proposed method achieves near-parity with centralized training using identical hyperparameters and achieves significant improvements over baseline local models.

Cavity magnomechanics offers an excellent platform for investigating macroscopic quantum phenomena by integrating magnons, phonons, and photons within one system. Distinctively, magnons inherently provide a nonlinear source for this category of networks. This nonlinear capability enables innovative strategies such as generating high-quality single and entangled photons, facilitating measurements with exceptional sensitivity, and synthesizing complex quantum states. This review summarizes current progress and prospective advancements in probe-light-based measurements aimed at sensing nonreciprocal magnon behaviors and generating entangled states. It specifically highlights the role of nonlinear phonon-magnon coupling, a mechanism essential for constructing quantum systems characterized by exceptional capacity in information storage and processing. Ultimately, this communication highlights promising avenues for future exploration within evolving coherent magnon-photon and phonon-magnon hybrid interfaces.

This paper presents a new reinforcement learning (RL) framework designed to enhance computational efficiency in quadrupedal locomotion by introducing an innovative foot trajectory generator that evolves paths. Traditionally, applying reinforcement learning for motion control necessitates rolling out thousands of simulation episodes; by constructing a motion optimizer instead, this method drastically reduces the required rollouts. The proposed approach functions in two distinct phases: first, it learns a generic foot trajectory generator capable of producing valid trajectories for any given command within a one-vs reinforcement learning process, followed by a second phase using a reward function that evaluates the evolutionary success of these trajectories. Our secondary component employs a genetic algorithm to generate a diverse population of foot trajectories for the trainer. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this method generates high-performance walking and running patterns, achieving performance levels superior to those obtained through standard RL training. Moreover, it facilitates the generation of novel footstep patterns. Ultimately, this research establishes a powerful RL-based approach for generating complex locomotion and a systematic pathway for creating innovative gait strategies.

Super-massive black holes (SMBHs), which range from $10^6$ to $10^9 M_{\odot}$, appear in both distant quasar systems and nearby galaxies. Those found in nearby environments are often observed in active galactic nuclei (AGNs) with very low luminosity, specifically $L_{\rm bol} \lesssim 10^{43} {\rm erg\ s^{-1}}$, indicating minimal activity levels. This subgroup is termed low-luminosity active galactic nuclei (LLAGNs). In these systems, LAGNs represent the majority of galactic nuclear black holes, posing significant challenges for researchers due to the difficulty in understanding their small-scale structures and the mechanisms driving their accretion and jets.

It employs the hybrid particle-in-cell (PIC)-fluid method, incorporating modern analytical theories of relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (RMHD) accretion and jet dynamics. The model utilizes analytical expressions for lags—delays in aligning electromagnetic fields with local plasma conditions caused by finite light travel time—and analyzes how these effects influence jet and accretion performance. In many real-world closed-loop systems, controllers are crafted through trial and error via reinforcement learning without ensuring specific performance criteria. These standards can instead be met more efficiently using model-based techniques that incorporate the laws of control theory. However, because existing models are rarely perfect in open-loop setups, any model-dependent changes will degrade controller performance unless the system remains in a closed-loop environment. Standard model predictive control strategies allow for iterative controller adjustments within these loops, yet reinvesting computational resources into process model estimation represents an unnecessary overhead. This paper presents new algorithms for simultaneous model identification and controller redesign that require zero computational cost for enhancing the model. We rigorously prove the stability of our proposed dynamic regulator and demonstrate through a simulation case study that this iterative, loop-closed approach significantly surpasses single-step methods in control performance.

The SiD Tracker represents a critical component of the proposed detector system currently under evaluation at the SLAC linear accelerator facility (SLA) for lepton colliders. A key design objective is achieving superior ionizing particle identification and precise measurement of primary vertex coordinates. To meet these goals, the tracker employs a SIlicon Drift Chamber (CDD), which features fine-scale electrode spacing, combined with proportional regions designed for ion collection optimization. This hybrid configuration prioritizes excellent spatial tracking capabilities, enabling accurate reconstruction of secondary collision products relevant to future experiments such as those at ILC or CLIC by delivering exceptional momentum precision, spatial resolution, and robust track resolution.

Using high-resolution spectra from the Gran Telescopio Canarias (GTC) at 850 nm, we conducted a detailed chemodynamical investigation of the globular cluster Tonozintla 2 (Ton2), located roughly 22 kiloparsecs away. Our study reveals approximately 30 new member stars, bringing the total analyzed sample to 108. Among these, 28 stars exhibit anomalous abundances not detectable in the standard atmospheric models used; specifically, 19 display enriched nitrogen levels and 6 show enrichment in either sodium or oxygen. The presence of a nitrogen-enriched subgroup suggests the existence of a second generation of stars within Ton2, characterized by an increased presence early on enclousured gas enriched in CNO-cycle elements from single- or double-star systems. Furthermore, we observe a clear anti-correlation between nitrogen and oxygen chemical ratios—a well-documented phenomenon in other clusters. Additionally, the oxygen variations among different subgroups within Ton2 provide circumstantial support for the theory that the observed Na-enriched group and Na-depleted (primary) population are distinct, offering direct evidence for chemical heterogeneity. Finally, by applying the anti-correlation rule, we successfully reconstructed a secondary composition for Ton2 that is fully consistent with previous observations of other major clusters.

Monitoring the state of the planet is vital for addressing global environmental, social, and economic challenges, as well as for forecasting their potential impacts. The accelerating volume of data generated by the numerous satellites deployed across various Earth observation programs now necessitates the creation of specialized infrastructure to support decision-making. We detail the design and architecture of the BODYSpace decision-making infrastructure—a purpose-built system developed for the European French Space Agency. This infrastructure was utilized to test the Earth Observation Data "tunnel," an initiative designed for continuous, real-time streaming of datasets vital for environmental change adaptation and prediction. Furthermore, we examine the findings from the demonstration of EO4Adapt, the benchmark application developed to validate this infrastructure.

We present a hydrodynamic framework for two-dimensional active nematic systems, allowing for an analysis of equilibrating properties. Surprisingly, this model reveals that nonlinearities in the equations of motion are marginally irrelevant, enabling us to derive closed-form expressions for the static two-point correlation functions for both nematic order and velocity fields, with integration limits spanning from zero to infinity. Furthermore, our hypothesis regarding the invariance of equilibrium properties under coordinate transformations has been validated across multiple dimensions and variable coordinate speeds.

Identifying irregular regions within spatio-temporal urban datasets constitutes a critical challenge for numerous real-world applications. Conventional methods address this by dividing urban areas into grid cells, after which anomaly detection algorithms analyze values within these partitions. However, these traditional techniques suffer from inherent gridification flaws, such as the arbitrary selection of grid sizes, resulting in uneven meshing. This leads to grid cells exhibiting spatio-temporally irrelevant values being treated as coherent entities. Furthermore, these methods often fail to effectively uncover anomalies exhibiting complex spatio-temporal patterns. An existing empirical evaluation confirms the limitations of current gridified approaches in accurately locating anomotic regions. To overcome these issues, this paper proposes Novel Anomaly Detection via Spatio-Temporal Pattern Reconstruction (NAD-STPR). This innovative framework bypasses gridification entirely by directly parsing the intrinsic, adaptive grid structure inherent in anomalies. By integrating domain-specific knowledge with advanced pattern recognition, NAD-STPR models the variable cellular mesh that characterizes distinct anomaly regions. Additionally, the approach employs an advanced algorithm to detect and track these adaptive cells. Ultimately, this method not only pinpoints anomotic regions but also provides diagnostics regarding their underlying spatio-temporal structural causes.

Typically, learning from source code involves either pre-defining operators and arguments or extensively pre-training models on vast datasets beforeconcentrating on a specific task. In contrast, this work tackles the challenge of learning graph representations for operators and arguments at once. While other research has explored using code execution for these models, this approach differs by also leveraging the structure of call graphs. Although the resulting method delivers performance gains, its primary contribution lies in demonstrating that the method defined by operator and argument sequences combined—the effective sequence of all first-degree subexpressions in a call graph where an operator appears as a node and its direct subexpressions as connected nodes—is inherently more rich and expressive than either component alone.

We present the first measurements of the stellar-to-halo mass relation (SHMR) specifically for early-type galaxies (ETGs), achieving this by statistically merging the weak-lensing (mass) and color–magnitude relations (age/dust) observed at redshifts between 0.2 and 2.0. Initial estimates derived from this method are corroborated using a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo approach, which separately calibrates the halo masses by accounting for photometric uncertainties and the non-linear correlations inherent between the color and luminosity of the galaxies. Our results align with standard SHMR expectations, peaking at approximately $\log M_{\rm {vir}} \simeq 12.6$ (a virial mass of roughly $4 \times 10^{12} \, \rm M_{\odot}$) and exhibiting peak specific stellar formation rates around $\log \left[ M_{\rm {vir}} / M_{\odot} \right] < 12.0$. Furthermore, the study investigates the SHMR for two distinct populations: red and quiescent ETGs and the "bluer," yet still quenched, trend of main-sequence star-forming ETGs. Although stellar photometry offers a cost-effective method for monitoring vertical aerosol optical depth (AOT), achieving high precision remains challenging. Limitations arise from atmospheric turbulence, detector noise, cloud coverage below the reference star, incorrect stellar selection, and difficulties in establishing a precise photometric reference due to turbulence. This study presents a proposal to overcome these barriers by adapting the concept of varying exposure lengths from solar imaging to ensure that each data point for every star is effectively normalized to its clear-sky counterpart. We name this approach the "clear sky normalization method." Monte Carlo simulations indicate that clear sky normalization significantly enhances data quality by producing outcomes consistent with one another, free from detector noise influences, and immune to turbulence-related errors regarding the photometric reference. Furthermore, we validated this technique using measurements taken by the Sion Stellar Photometer at Sion Observatory in Switzerland, demonstrating that the clarity of each result can be substantially improved through this correction.

We present GGLasso, an R package offering seamless integration of the Graphical Lasso algorithm for statistical analysis as well as graphically visualizing the resulting graphical models. Graphical Lasso serves as a regularization technique designed to recover the sparse inverse of a multivariate Gaussian distribution's covariance matrix. In graphical terms, a non-zero entry in this inverted matrix signifies a direct edge between two variables in a high-dimensional sparse undirected graph. This comprehensive library supports users in efficiently computing and exploring these sparse graph structures.

This study presents theoretical modeling comparing photoevaporation with advection-driven accretion to explain the emission profile of a T Tauri star, utilizing the MAPE (Multi-Accretion PhotoEvaporation) code which simulates an accretion shock and a photoevaporating, spherically expanding wind. First, a model incorporating photoevaporation and an accretion shock was developed and calibrated against observational data for the TW Hydrae disk, with a specific accretion rate of $5 \times 10^{-9} M_{\odot} yr^{-1}$. Subsequently, a comparative advective accretion model was advanced, yielding an inverted near-infrared (NIR) profile consistent with IR observational flux of TW Hydrae. A subsequent comparison indicates both theoretical frameworks plausibly fit the NIR photometry of TW Hydrae; however, only the photoevaporation model successfully accounts for the ultraviolet (UV) emissions. Applying MAPE parameters to TW IK2, a secondary disk system, yielded similar findings. While a single photoevaporation wind model did not perfectly replicate all disk properties, a dual wind configuration featuring an accelerated shear flow effectively simulated its characteristics. In both systems, the proposed model demonstrates that photoevaporation plays a critical role in shaping the disk and driving the inflow of matter toward the central star.

Detecting voiced speech, estimating the pitch contour, and classifying harmonic speech are crucial components for numerous speech technology applications. Within our study, we present specialized deep neural network methods for addressing the interconnected challenges of voiced speech detection along with pitch and harmonic-ness estimation. These techniques perform effectively across varied acoustical environments and are robust to different speech types. Key findings include a novel deep learning approach to voiced speech detection that surpasses existing state-of-the-art algorithms by an average of ~15.15% in detection accuracy. Additionally, we introduce three lightweight models—each based on comparatively simple architectural components—that simultaneously satisfy the needs of detection and pitch estimation. These models exhibit computational parameters constituting only a small fraction of those required by current leading solutions.

We introduce a new Dual-proimal Proximity Gradient (DWP) method for solving structured convex optimization challenges. While the widely used Chambolle-Pock primal-dual algorithm and its variants rely on linear operators to balance simplicity and broad applicability—often failing with certain nonlinear setups—we demonstrate how adapting both algorithms to handle nonlinear conditions becomes feasible. This results in our proposed DWP framework, which converges for a significantly wider range of convex problems and supports stopping criteria tailored to general non-convergent scenarios.

Recent years have seen neural architecture search (NAS) emerge as a pivotal technique for automatically creating deep learning models. While current methodologies typically function within rigidly structured design spaces, these methods often overlook the broad, open-ended landscapes found in nature. This paper introduces a groundbreaking approach for navigating these complex, neural architecture spaces using reinforcement learning. By training on a wide array of configurations, our method effectively identifies both highly performant and diverse designs. Tested in an space spanning over one billion possibilities, the technique produced top-class models that rival those from previous restricted search domains, while also generating a significant variety of alternative architectures. Crucially, this capability for generating varied yet competent models makes the technique particularly suited for applications demanding robustness and reliability. Finally, the study demonstrates that transferring these architectures to various computer vision tasks yields positive outcomes.

Multicast beamforming is essential for enhancing spectral efficiency in future wireless networks; however, determining its impact on overall system performance remains challenging due to the intricate nature of the underlying optimization framework. This study addresses the issue by providing insights into multicast beamforming effects on spectral efficiency. Specifically, we demonstrate that optimal solutions can be derived by decomposing the aggregate message set into distinct subgroups, each served with independent beamformers known as group transmission sets (GTTs), while simultaneously utilizing full-dimensional transmission sets (FTTs) for each GTT. Each component set is optimized individually to maximize a specific spectral efficiency metric derived from the total rate. Consequently, the count of GTT with FTAs is constrained only by system requirements, allowing these configurations to be determined with relative computational ease compared to tackling a multi-variable problem. Furthermore, the decomposition is structured such that the resulting spectral efficiency approaches an achievable performance bound as fewer message subgroups are employed. Simulation results illustrate that employing a transmission scheme combining group and full transmissions—where some groups are sent via separate beamformers while the rest share resources—often yields higher spectral efficiency than utilizing full transmission for all messages.

Communication bottlenecks constitute a significant obstacle to the widespread adoption of Federated Learning. Federated Distillation addresses this challenge by enhancing communication efficiency through model output prediction rather direct parameter aggregation. In this paper, we investigate distinct variants of Federated Distillation and evaluate their potential for real-world deployment. Our analysis reveals substantial communication advantages of these methods, and we assert Federated Distillation is a highly promising approach to mitigate the issues associated with limited bandwidth in federated settings.

Named Data Networking (NDN) represents a promising architecture for evolving distributed computing networks, operating by providing content-centric data delivery. In this model, applications request specific content based on a "Named Data" principle, receiving relevant information while bypassing unnecessary data transmission caused by semantic ambiguity. This paper details an initial exploration of "Content-Aware NDN" applications, focusing on the implementation strategy that targets precise data relevance to enhance efficiency. We introduce the framework, architecture, and underlying principles required to harness the full potential of this capability. Initial experiments within an emulation environment validate the feasibility of this approach, with application scenarios expected to yield future performance gains.

This research addresses the unresolved question of exponential stability for a specific Euler–Bernoulli beam model described on a metric graph with three uniform arms radiating in a star configuration. The outer vertices are simply supported (hinged), whereas the central node allows both longitudinal displacement and angular rotation. The stability analysis relies on inputting time-dependent forcing functions at the left two outers supports. The primary contributions are the derivation of a well-posed strong solution and the formal asymptotic expansion for long-term behavior. It transpires that this system's eigenvalues lack associated eigenvectors; their spectral analysis reveals a spectrum resembling a classical arithmetic ladder. The construction of these non-standard spectral elements hinges on specific relations linking the central beam's eigenvectors to those of two simplified harmonic oscillators. The analysis suggests that exponential stability occurs if and only if a specific arithmetic relation binds the beam's flexural rigidity to the lengths of the first two arms, with the corresponding decay rate being directly proportional to the magnitude of this arithmetic defect. This finding generalizes prior specific-case results from literature involving a stretched Euler–Bernoulli beam on an interval bounded by two "waterwheel" (combination of clamped and clamped-rotational) boundaries. The current framework can be extended to graphs with $N \geq 3$ uniform arms situated at arbitrary branching angles at a single intersection point across various boundary conditions. This study examines whether inhomogeneous chiral phases exist within the quark-meson model, which incorporates explicit chiral-symmetry breaking. Results indicate that although the region permitting these inhomogeneities diminishes as pion mass increases, such phases persist at the physical pion mass. Furthermore, instability driving inhomogeneous matter formation manifests in the scalar channel, as opposed to the less favorable pseudoscalar modes.

Current multi-objective optimization techniques typically rely on a fixed utility function, predetermined by expert input, or employ a small number of agents to guide the search. However, predefined functions often fail to capture nuanced preferences due to the intricate nature of the optimization landscape, while limited agent populations lack the diversity necessary for an effective search. This study introduces an iterative process designed to elict precise preference information from clients regarding search direction, a function grounded in machine learning that analyzes the client's historical data interactions. Our strategy is utility-free; it requires no initial utility function and can accommodate multiple, potentially conflicting objectives. Furthermore, the learning algorithm's output utilizes virtual "imaginee" agents with distinct percepts of the problem space to learn and refine their shared strategies. Crucially, we demonstrate that these refined strategies effectively reflect the client's true preferences by utilizing the imaginees as intermediaries, thereby avoiding any need to directly expose the client to the search for utility definitions.

Recent studies have demonstrated that neural-network-dependent RL agents are vulnerable to adversarially perturbed inputs that cause significant performance drops. Although prior work examined attack types like poisoning or physical deception, this research investigates "on-the-fly" adversarial attacks alongside defense strategies within on-policy agents—a notably more challenging scenario involving online learning updates to the policy network. We present findings confirming the susceptibility of such agents to on-the-fly attacks in control tasks like robotic swinging and demonstrate that simple defense methods maintain robustness by either avoiding or correcting the adversarial inputs. Specifically, we propose an unsupervised proximity-based filter to discard corrupted inputs and a reference-based normalization technique to utilize agent memory. Unlike the former, which increases susceptibility to attacks by discarding inputs, the latter avoids such vulnerabilities. Applied to robotic balancing scenarios, our methods enable reliable robot operation despite continuous on-the-fly attacks, achieving up to 8000 successful episode completions.

We investigate the spectral properties of a low-symmetry 2D electronic lattice modeled by a tight-binding framework. Within this model, we identify topological band gaps as well as non-trivial topological invariants defined by the first and second Chern numbers. Unlike the conventional honeycomb lattice that exhibits multiple Dirac cones, our proposed structure forms a square-based unit cell; consequently, it lacks higher-order band degeneracies characteristic of that system. We define the model's Hamiltonian using a linear parameter set for ease of identification with experimental setups and demonstrate through numerical analysis the presence of momentum-dependent band gaps. Specifically, we utilize contour plots of effective hopping amplitude and band structures to establish the precise topological phase diagram of the system. Furthermore, we introduce the method of unit cell transformation to adjust the unit cell's geometry, thereby facilitating the creation of Topological Dirac Cones (TDCs) via the strategic selection of appropriate topological phases.

In non-stochastic reinforcement learning settings where environments undergo gradual shifts, maintaining near-optimal performance demands agent-specific adaptation. This research extends the Moneyline family of risk-aware RL algorithms, which are currently limited to completely stochastic task settings, by applying them to non-stationary tasks. Even when not required, an explicit change budget enhances computational and space efficiency. The extended moneyline methods retain the variance budget's efficiency for non-stationary tasks and further a new bound on the optimal long-term average reward for such non-stationar settings. The extended methods also maintain the original risk-awareness. The extended moneylines perform well across both a stochastic task and a non-stationar task with a known budget and meet performance targets using less exploration, as the user can control how the system learns based on the known budget of changes. The extended moneylines also perform well across two simulation tasks to demonstrate their effectiveness and efficiency in these diverse environments.

Organizations have shifted toward project management tools that integrate multiple data sources, including issue tracking systems. These systems serve as a centralized repository for general progress notes, allowing users to incorporate detailed insights into activity logs via references and summaries. This research investigates the correlation between issues and historical activity details, a area previously explored but not scaled to real-world organizational data. We present analysis across four issues involving activity references from one major technology organization. Findings highlight that compiled progress notes offer rich, underutilized data for identifying patterns; this paper suggests specific data mining techniques to extract such patterns and issue-specific details from these records.

Distributed machine learning (DML) across time-varying networks enables emerging applications like autonomous driving and mobile device processing, where offline and centralised online methods are unfeasible. Unlike robustly studied robust equilibrium points in standard distributed learning, the convergence behaviour and performance of gradient descent (GD) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) against malicious nodes remain uncharacterized. Addressing this gap, we provide a comprehensive analysis of how these algorithms withstand byzantine attacks. By defining the convergence set of both methods under adversarial influence, we establish that their stationary behaviours consist of combinations of global minima and local minimal values, with specific weights for each based on the fraction of corrupted nodes. Consequently, our work establishes the theoretical resilience of GD and SGD against maleficient nodes, while the accompanying codebase is publicly available at https://github.com/jianyuz/DSGDLBYZ.

This study introduces an on-chip multi-grating apparatus designed to bridge single atoms and integrated photonics by directing and trapping single Rubidium atoms using an optical optical dipole trap (ODT). The device funnels atoms from a sub-micron Raman-Našek atom source along a defined trajectory to a mesoscopic trap formed by six coherent superposed Bessel beams. These beams are generated through the use of a conical near-field transformation lens and a corresponding conical convection in the free-electron region prior to surface, guiding them toward the target location. The resulting trap has a diameter of approximately 1.1 µm and resides about 11 µm above the overall platform. The proposed method offers the foundation for future research into the interaction between single atoms and photonics, specifically through a compact single quantum system combining matter and light interfaces.

Artificial neural networks are widely leveraged for predicting chemical properties from molecular structure, thereby accelerating the design of novel compounds with tailored attributes. However, current practices often neglect amino acids during this process. We address this by introducing a new approach that utilizes amino acids—specifically their side chains, as full sequences are too lengthy—to forecast protein characteristics. We propose optimizing side chain orientations for short peptides to enhance function or minimize toxicity within cell cultures and living organisms. We developed SideChainResNet, a side chain prediction tool derived from ResNet, which outperforms the non-neural baseline "SideChain-RNN." Furthermore, we demonstrate through in vitro and in vivo experiments the feasibility of engineering peptides with side chains optimized to interact with small molecular compounds.

Dynamics-optimization problems involving continuous time, where an analytical solution cannot be derived numerically, require solution through direct transcription into discrete time. This paper presents a methodology for approximating near-optimal state and control trajectories by formulating a continuous-time cost function with point-wise constraints, then solving a corresponding weighted least-squares system. This approach is adaptable to both open- and closed-loop formulations. Solvability and approximate optimality are ensured by demonstrating the conditions for the convergence of the sequences generated by this process. Furthermore, a specific algorithm for computing these sequence sequences is introduced.

A rational function $f$ defined over the extended complex plane $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ with precisely two critical points corresponds to a bicritical map. Up to the action of Möbius transformations, there exist countably many finitely many conjugacy classes for such maps; specifically, non-finly critical maps fall into exactly two classes. For any given bicritical map with all posts critically and one-to-many, there is an associated parameter space where every value defines a unique dynamics. The current research introduces two different families of these maps—the so-called *Chebyshev* and *Newton* maps—each organized into tailored parameter spaces. The authors establish the topological structure of these spaces, identifying exactly when each map exhibits hyperbobic behavior and separates these functional forms. Furthermore, they classify the parameter subsets producing known critical families, including post-critically finite maps and multiplication-quations.

We investigate comprehensive Bayesian methods applied to high-dimensional linear regression by adopting data-driven empirical priors. This class of priors offers favorable posterior contraction properties, enabling precise inference even when the number of predictors far surpasses the number of observations. Unlike other shrinkage priors whose parameters are tuned using marginal fit—potentially causing bias in high settings—the suggested empirical priors feature automatic posterior contraction. Such behavior leads to superior sampling distributions and more reliable marginal posterior densities compared to alternative shrinkage solutions. Many individuals underestimate the privacy risks associated with uploading photos to the internet. This paper introduces the Graph Privacy Advisor, an application that acts as an image privacy classifier. It predicts privacy status by analyzing scene details and the number of objects present. To achieve better results with a simpler architecture, the system enhances the relevance of extracted image data. This strategy effectively reduces bias while simultaneously improving the classifier's accuracy.

I develop and numerically solve a radiation model based on the nonlinear Schrödinger equation to examine radiative self-interaction and the consequences for quantum decay. The analysis demonstrates that quantum effects enable a particle to dynamically couple with its own history, allowing it to distinctly perceive previous states. Numerical solutions reveal that while long-term asymptotic behavior remains unchanged in the presence of radiative coupling compared to the non-relativistic case, the evolution of intermediate states differs notably due to self-interaction with the particle's trail. Consequently, while theory predicts that individual decay events should exhibit shorter lifespans due to increased interaction, this specific effect is anticipated to be minimal for particles like the muon due to their inherently quantum nature.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider utilized $pp$ data of 20 $\text{pb}^{-1}$ at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV to analyse functions of nearly balanced inclusive jet pairs event, requiring at least one tagged photon. Research focused on multiple fragmentation functions (FFs) of charged particles within a proximity radius of 0.4, comparing the photon-tagged sample against an unbiased inclusive jet sample. In photon-tagged events, FFs exhibited elevated charged particle counts relative to inclusive events as energy increased. The study proceeded to evaluate the validity of the modified leading particle hypothesis in photon-tagged events; this hypothesis suggested particle multiplicity should remain equal between the two datasets. The findings revealed significant deviations from this hypothesis for the majority of particles, indicating its invalidity under these conditions. These results served to test the adequacy of parton shower models as implemented in the PYTHIA8 event simulator.

Solar atmospheric observations reveal highly dynamic and intense magnetic field lines, indicating significant internal energy dynamics within the corona. Nanoflares, small energy bursts hypothesized by Parker as the primary heat source for the corona, have been detected more consistently in recent years across various solar instruments and electromagnetic bands and magnetic configurations. Beyond heating, nanoflares likely contribute to coronal mass dynamics and variability. This paper provides a detailed analysis of predicted nanoflare signatures based on magnetic field theory and offers guidance for observational strategies to detect and quantify them effectively.

Data augmentation is increasingly recognized as an essential technique for enhancing the representation learning of graph neural networks. In this work, we introduce a novel method tailored for predicting social influence that performs data augmentation on social influence graphs. While existing graph analysis approaches often rely on reconstructing node labels to improve model performance, this approach is unsupervised because accurate influence values are difficult to obtain. Instead, our graph is augmented through the integration of side information that reflects social node attributes. Following reconstruction and training on these augmented structures, our method effectively improves social influence prediction and generalizes state-of-the-art performance.

This study presents an accessible derivation of the Cramér-Rao lower bound (CRLB) specifically tailored for pose estimation scenarios. The approach treats pose estimation as a general multivariate problem, formulating the estimator's measurement model around a set of three-dimensional unit vectors with known relationships to one another. By calculating the CRLB, the authors determine the minimum theoretical bounds for the estimation errors of these vectors. The findings demonstrate that this estimation accuracy limit remains invariant to rotations but changes according to shifts in position. Furthermore, the paper evaluates the performance of the Least Squares estimator by comparing its error bounds against our derived CRLB. We also extend the analysis to the Maximum Likelihood estimator by proposing methods to calculate its specific CRLB. Ultimately, numerical comparisons confirm that the maximum likelihood estimator consistently achieves accuracy that aligns precisely with the predicted limits.

Various models rooted in string theory and supergravity feature hidden sectors that significantly impact cosmology and particle physics, with dark matter potentially residing within these sectors in principle. We explore a scenario in which a specific dynamic form of dark energy arises from the collective modulation by fermions or scalars – also present in the hidden sector – serving simultaneously as dark energy and dark matter. We outline key physical and mathematical constraints on this dark energy scenario within a supergravity framework and demonstrate that, by leveraging the extensive freedom available in hidden sector constructions, a broad spectrum of viable solutions exists to satisfy these constraints.

This work details an analysis of simulated same-sign W boson production within proton-proton collisions occurring at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, utilizing the ATLAS detector. An inclusive dataset representing 37 fb$^{-1}$ was analyzed to establish an data-centric selection framework for specific kinematic properties of the two charged lepton-W boson pairs, specifically targeting events with exactly four charged leptons (electrons or muons) in the final state (after excluding Z boson decays), alongside reconstructed or kinematically inferred W bosons. The study derives both data and simulation-based normalization factors by comparing template-fitted normalization distributions against template-fitted background-subtracted data distributions across four disjoint p$_\mathrm{T}$ regions of reconstructed or kinematically inferred W bosons, respectively. Furthermore, this research presents a first template-fitted extraction of same-sign W boson event yields using this specific lepton-centric selection method and compares these measured luminosities against established Standard Model predictions.

This paper introduces an end-to-end framework for the first time enhances monochrome cameras with the capabilities of their paired color counterparts. Because the color and monochrome sensors operate both spatially and temporally in parallel, the input image pairs exhibit variations in lighting intensity and chromatic information. The processing pipeline consists of four stages: (1) aligning the images in space and time (2) transferring missing RGB values into the monoscopic input using a conditional diffusion model; (3) generating missing textures via a diffusion-based image editing system powered by human prompts; and (4) re-texturizing the resulting image with style retexturization with style control (RSTCR). The final output is a complete colorized image adapted to match the original scene characteristics. Extensive testing shows that utilizing this method improves Perceptual Image Quality Assessment scores by up to 13%. The code is available at https://github.com/HKBU-MLLab/CamBridge.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has emerged as an effective strategy to mitigate data sparsity and enhance recommendation performance by leveraging transfer learning from auxiliary domains. Yet, prevailing cross-domain techniques often rely on single-domain or sparse-domain-based methods that fail to fully exploit abundant, disjoint dense datasets, thereby limiting their potential. Addressing this limitation, we introduce the Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) model. MSDCR explicitly exploits the available disjoint dense domains as guides to achieve higher-quality representation learning from these sources. Furthermore, the model incorporates a multi-sparse-domain interaction module to capture domain-specific characteristics and infer relevant information across these disjoint datasets. Experimental validation conducted on two real-world datasets demonstrates that MSDCR consistently surpasses state-of-the-art alternatives.

Local magnetic moments appear consistently in disordered insulators like Si1-xCxx:3 where electron doping of an n-type semiconductor drives it through the Bose-Einstein condensation of aligned spins into a polarized state, erasing local moments at the critical doping level $x_c$. This transition from localized to polarized behavior can also occur by increasing temperature above $T_c$ during continuous doping or by maintaining constant temperature and increasing the dislocation density via high-dislocation material engineering. This final preparation method represents a novel synthesis technique. This study examines correlations in the resulting random singlet phase from continuous doping of bulk SiGe materials using muon spin rotation techniques to reveal that either increasing the dislocation density or elevating the temperature results in a logarithmic temporal decay of these correlations, a signature distinct from local moment behaviors.

The Optimal Generating System (OGS) strategy addresses the difficulty of uniquely representing all group elements using the shortest possible sequence of generator words. Currently, only two methods are known to be optimal: one applies specifically to abelian groups, featuring OGS structures based on binary numbers, while the other targets small, non-abelian groups, defined by the four-letter relators of the Lazy Lazy Group (LLG). While the former guarantees a group element representation with polynomial word growth, the latter results in exponential growth for these smaller non-abelian cases. This research introduces a generalized OGS OGS framework capable of handling both abelian and "most" non-abelian groups. By doing so, it defines an OGS that yields only exponential growth in these contexts, though it also establishes the boundaries—specifically identifying the precise set of groups—within which this particular generalization remains valid for proving uniqueness and optimality of the resulting system.

Robots employing inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to acquire skills from demonstrations may encounter disruptive events, such as malfunctions during execution. While previous work addressed IRL with noisy observations by assuming these disruptions are random and unpredictable, we investigate scenarios where they are both correlated with observation points and non-stochastic. We prove that certain noises can completely undermine standard IRL approaches and existing variations by introducing noise metadata as part of the data set. Given the inherent difficulty of distinguishing noise from genuine observations of a perfect agent based on correlated data, we propose a two-step solution: initially, employ standard outlier detection algorithms on the metadata to identify noisy segments; subsequently, filter these detected outliers from the observation collection before applying conventional IRL. Experimental validation using both simulated scenarios and a physical robotic arm demonstrates the efficacy of this approach compared to current noisy observation methods.

We propose a two-phased deep reinforcement learning algorithm designed for resolving demanding control tasks. While deep learning has proven successful for high-dimensional environments, it often struggles with sample inefficiency and instability when learning precise terminal rewards in settings with sparse rewards or when exact cost functions are undefined. To overcome these barriers, our "World Model Guided Reinforcement Learning" (WMGRL) strategy splits the process into distinct stages. The initial world model phase involves training a model capable of predicting system dynamics within the given environment. Subsequently, this world model serves as a proxy for guiding control policy iteration, significantly enhancing sample utility. Notably, this approach does not require a dynamic programming solution or direct minimization of an exact cost function; instead, it incorporates the world model itself as a core component of the policy's cost structure. This world model helps stabilize the learning process and remains effective even when performance metrics are vague. The framework encompasses various neural dynamics and policy formulations, illustrated through a concrete locomotion application featuring a 3D environment with seven-degree-of-freedom inputs and multi-dimensional outputs, demonstrating its versatility.

Robust research data management stands as a cornerstone of contemporary laboratory operations, a challenge that current tools address only partially; specific software is often lacking in the realm of chemistry. Existing general-purpose laboratory platforms are not always aligned with the workflows of chemical researchers, whereas electronic diaries fail to support deductive research driven by data without further hindering other fields. To bridge this specific knowledge and methodology in chemistry, we introduce Data-driven Deductive Research in Chemistry (D^2RAC), a freely accessible, multi-user system designed for chemical labs. D^2RAC integrates seamlessly with standard equipment including micro-titration setups, micro-plate readers, micro-weighing balances, and micro-plate incubators. By facilitating the organized, structured capture of laboratory notebooks alongside experiment data, the platform automates routine administrative tasks and enhances the efficiency, clarity, and replicability of experimental procedures, thereby enhancing utility, transparency, and understanding of findings.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), characterized as multi-component materials with multiple main constituents comprising over 5 to 10 elements, have garnered significant interest within the scientific community for their exceptional mechanical properties and versatile functional characteristics. Probabilistic frameworks and unsupervised methods for latent variable learning and representation are unified into a single model, defined by a joint distribution over hidden variables and a set of functions that define the joint distribution over these latent variables and their corresponding observations. We address two primary objectives within this framework: estimating the latent state based on current observations and using this learning capability for prediction. We have developed the Expectation-Construction Switching Reduction (EC-SVR) algorithm—a novel method to approximate marginal distributions and recover previous variational approaches by exactly solving these optimization problems. Evaluation on synthetic data demonstrates performance comparable to established baseline models, with EC-SVR exhibiting superior convergence rate characteristics relative to existing solutions.

The nonlinearity of a multivariational Boolean function quantifies how effectively it masks affine transformations. Previous literature established that the maximum nonlinearity for an $n$-variable function with vector output of length $m$ is capped at $\left(\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{4}\sqrt{\frac{m}{2}}\right)^{2}n$, a limit achieved solely when the columns of the corresponding Sabot matrix are drawn from Sidon sets. The authors introduce a novel class of low-linear functions designed with an optimized structure and efficient speed. They also provide a general design method for incrementing functionarity while preserving low-linearity characteristics. The system's efficiency is verified through both analytical proofs and computational simulations. Moreover, the work demonstrates that the newly proposed Sabot sets yield functions with higher linearity than any existing Sabon-set-derived functions to date.

Binary matrices are ubiquitous in science and industry, yet generating unbiased random samples of an arbitrary submatrix remains both computationally demanding and practically hard to access. While reading issues are common because access patterns may skew the selected submatrix, the challenge persists for applications like anonymizing sensitive datasets. This study introduces two new Swapping Algorithms—both direct Rook and generalized variants—to address these issues. Our primary contribution is the analytical swapping probability theorem proving that structural zeros drastically reduce the swapping probability for those cells. Consequently, samples drawn from regions with high concentrations of structural zeros approximate an ideal, uniform distribution of swap events. Experimental results confirm direct Rook samplers achieve near-uniform swap rates across all rows and columns in most tested scenarios, while the generalized approach performs optimally in contexts featuring complex connectivity that direct methods struggle with, offering superior results there as well as efficiency gains over previous methods.

Achieving reliable fitting of Parton Distribution Function (PDFs) demands the unification of multiple data sources, including experimental datasets and non-perturbative results from the lattice QCD, with theoretical predictions like those for PDFs derived from lattice QCD and cross-section calculations. While modern experimental fitting frameworks, such as those used by the PDF4All group, efficiently handle large and diverse datasets, they typically overlook these predictive models. Conversely, code bases like FastFit, designed to accommodate these predictions, struggle with minor defects in input data, lacking robust error handling, and finding it difficult to process the massive real-world data dumps effectively. To address this gap, we present UniFit, a unified, didactic, and practical software package engineered to fit PDFs by harmonizing lattice QCD PDFs, experimental data, theoretical loop predictions, perturbation QCD (pQCD) calculations, process predictions, parton showers, and global averaging models. UniFit features two key components: first, an extended version of FastFit capable of managing experimental data alongside lattice QCD PDFs and various perturbation QCD predictions, while also providing statistical error estimation; second, UniFit-MC, a dedicated module that integrates Monte Carlo methods with MC modules. This dual-component structure ensures both flexibility and accuracy in fitting procedures.

We explored the parametric seeding of microcombs utilizing a two electrooptic modulator-based offset frequency lock technique, featuring an extended control range by over two orders of magnitude compared to traditional methods. We implemented two distinct feedback strategies to extend this control range: one based on direct electrostatic actuation of a resonator and another on feedback-driven adjustment of modulators. This approach enables active tuning of microcombs through electric fields, offering a promising alternative to conventional methods that rely on varying microcavity temperatures.

Extending the contributions of Sun and Kechris-Quording, we show that every acylindrically hyperbolic group possesses a faithful, weakly mixing probability-measure-preserving action that fails to be essentially free. Similarly, we introduce that every non-elementary hyperbolic group admits a random subroup with these identical properties: a characteristic random subgroup that is faithful, weakly mixing, yet essentially not free, or equivalently, its weak mixing does imply essential freedom.

Quantized neural networks have recently drawn significant research attention due to their ability to lower storage requirements and accelerate inference; however, there is a persistent debate within deep learning regarding how quantization influences generalization. Our study presents a deep characterization of this effect. By integrating probabilistic bounds with deep learning theories, we demonstrate that for a broad class of activation functions, quantized neural networks with bounded weights suffer from an inherent generalization deficit compared to traditional models using unlimited real-valued weights. Specifically, we show that for activation functions with subgaussian derivatives, the minimization of an empirical risk over a quantized model class yields upper bounds on the true risk for test data elevated by at least a term proportional to *b/s*, where *b* denotes the bit width of the quantized weights and *s* represents the sample count. Consequently, this establishes theoretically that quantized neural networks are strictly harder to generalize within the framework of finite sampling. Through extensive experiments, we examine this phenomenon in both data classification and natural language processing tasks, providing both theoretical insight and practical details, including strategies to alleviate the observed generalization hurdles.

Quantum states with geometric counterparts in the bulk allow for the exploration of how quantum information theories interact with gravitational models. This study investigates the consistency of bulk duals regarding multipartite entanglement theories, specifically deriving new constraints on bulk entropies by adapting the definition of the Holographic Entropy Cone from the Journal Reference: arXiv:2203.02034. These derived constraints were found to align perfectly with the original cone, implying that bulk entropies must adhere strictly to these rules; this discovery implies a mapping where every state dual to a bulk has its boundary entropy structure also satisfying such cones under geometric translation. Furthermore, this work analyzes how violating these entropy constraints would force deviations in information theories on the boundary. Extending this analysis, the authors introduce the concept of the Boundary Entropy Cone, which shares key similarities with the bulk version but incorporates unique characteristics arising from the boundary's structure.

Signal recovery methods within the framework of compressed sensing frequently benefit from normalization techniques. At a conceptual level, these methods aim to address specific deficiencies arising from restricted constraints; practically, they serve as regularizers that guide recovery algorithms. In this work, we investigate their role in accelerating coordinate descent techniques for compressed sensing. By introducing an efficient proximal solver for a proposed nuclear norm-based regularized minimization problem, we propose a regularization-based scheme to enhance Compressive Minimax Convolution. Experimental results demonstrate improved signal recovery success rates, speed, and robustness against noise. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a carefully selected regularizer can significantly accelerate the coordinate descent process.

Tracing the evolution of cell shapes is essential for understanding cells themselves and deciphering the mechanisms driving their movements. While voxels are commonly used to represent cell shapes, they often lack the spatial and temporal precision required for accurate biological modeling and are generally unsuited for numerical simulation. Conversely, polygon meshes are effective at providing high-resolution shape tracking with good temporal and spatial precision; but this comes at the cost of significant memory consumption and computational inefficiency during simulations. This paper demonstrates that using level sets on signed distance functions (SDFs) offers an optimal compromise for these constraints. We developed a novel algorithm for simulating cell dynamics using an SF-driven approach (often called "sf-voxels"), where cells are defined as the region where the SDF value is negative. This method defines both spatial and temporal resolution directly by selecting SDF voxel dimensions, allowing for significantly smaller, dynamically resolved time steps. Because the level set voxel boundary consistently stays within the original SDF grid and does not dictate simulation outcomes, we created a boundary detection algorithm that smoothly transitions from an interior representation to external space. Neuroscience research indicates that spatial navigation relies on several non-Cartesian representations beyond the standard Euclidean framework. As computational limitations extend robot operations beyond protected environments, it becomes critical to comprehend how these alternative representations support spatial perception and navigation. This study investigates the capabilities offered by a metric graph representation for continuous navigation tasks using a simulated agent equipped with omnidirectional sensory input. The agent moves through environments structured as two-dimensional maps but lacks prior topological knowledge, relying solely on local sensory data to infer global configuration. We observe the agent's emergence of a self-organized, grid-like representation of its own layout within this framework. Subsequent analysis compares its inferred graph structure against a ground-traveling algorithm's known version. The results demonstrate the agent's capacity to accurately map unexplored areas while simultaneously maintaining a robust internal model of its own topology.

This study benchmarks event-chain Monte Carlo (ECMC) algorithms against the local reversible Metropolis (MR) algorithm for simulating rigid spheres under hard-sphere conditions. While both approaches function within a configurational space defined by particle coordinates and a Lagrange multiplier representing cell volume, only the non-reversible ECMC variant demonstrates significant efficiency gains. Specifically, the integration of a continuously driven test particle and its associated momentum transfer into the acceptance criterion constitutes a fundamental structural difference between ECMC and MR. Despite potential volume update slowings due longer correlation times, we observe that particle-displacement-based acceptance in ECMC yields marked acceleration over standard Metropolis sampling at a given system density. This efficiency scales well with increasing particle count due to the algorithm's independence from acceptance rates. To fully realize its potential within compressed fluid simulations, further advancements in how the cell volume dynamics are handled remain necessary.

Sound Event Localization and Detection (SELD) involves identifying acoustic sources and determining their positions, a capability vital for robots and assistive audio systems. Most existing methods for solving this problem employ convolutional recurrent neural networks (CRNNs) processing multi-microphone magnitude spectra as time-frequency slides to estimate the time-frequency masks necessary for isolating specific sounds. This approach has proven limited by the constant channel width constraint inherent in slide-based slides, which stops the model from integrating larger contextual information. Wide-CRNN enables the integration of broader context within frequency domains, while Planar-CRNN facilitates the passage of two-dimensional time-frequency maps across a network. We further broaden the concept of masks through novel designs in the time and delay-energy domains, integrating these new representations into our architectures. We assessed performance using extended versions of the Pandora and DCMoSE datasets. Our experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over current baseline models across all evaluated metrics.

Recent research has highlighted a dichotomy in El Niño-Easterly Oscillation (ENSO) types, defined by the longitudinal extent of sea surface temperature (SST) anomalies. This study employs a deterministic, traveling wave-derived wave packet model to analyze how these categories influence global seasonal precipitation. An eastern Pacific (EP) wave packet, designed to align with key EP ENSO traits, produces distinct remote precipitation responses. In contrast, a western Pacific (CP)—referenced as the Western Pacific central ENSO type in source—travels south and triggers significant seasonal rainfall shifts across Indonesia and the Malay Archipelago. Although both EP and CP ENSO variants induce similar seasonal precipitation changes in the tropical Pacific region and equatorial Atlantic, the EP type elicits more robust patterns over Europe, Africa, and North America. The findings indicate that EP ENSO accounts for seasonal precipitation variability across most examined regions of the globe.

By modeling the tidal stripping of initial accretion disks surrounding early dwarf galaxies—which subsequently accreted material to form their current SMBHs—we estimate the density and velocity dispersion of tidal streams and their cores. Additionally, to support future missions like *SKA* and *薇龙* (薇龙), which aim to detect millisecond pulsars (MSPs), we calculate the anticipated discovery rate of MSPs arising from dry mergers and dry mergers within dwarf galaxies. Our results offer quantitative predictions designed to back upcoming observables dedicated to understanding the origins of massive black holes found in dwarf galaxies.

The dynamics of wide binary (WB) stars provide a unique opportunity to validate gravity theories under the extremely low accelerations characteristic of a galaxy's peripheral regions. Existing modeling frameworks for knowledge-intensive business processes lack support for separating semi- from fully automated flows, a hurdle essential for implementing systematic collaboration between humans and machines. To bridge this gap, our proposal introduces shared process structures and a dual-execution model capable of handling both complete workflows and partially automated tasks. Furthermore, our work tackles synchronization challenges in regions involving manual activities, a problem not addressed in prior related work for fully automated contexts. Ultimately, our methodology facilitates the automated extraction of performance metrics from partially automated processes and enables more precise scheduling and resource allocation during the planning phase.

Frequent wildfires significantly impact solar energy output by altering atmospheric conditions; these fires release vast amounts of aerosols that scatter and absorb sunlight, thereby reducing irradiance at the surface. These instance instances are defined by vectors of i.i.d. components drawn from a zero-mean multivariate Gaussian distribution, sparse due to dimensionality reduction, and acyclosely connected. We establish that the average-case complexity relies on the concentration profile of eigenvalues near the boundaries of the expected spectral distribution of the Hessian matrix along the manifold of the graph's polygon space. Specifically, the average performance ratio for two heuristics—the matrix Hessian and the Hessian thresholding methods—depends on this eigenvalue boundary concentration. We provide initial averages-case results for these heuristics and detail average-case analysis approaches for other problems defined on the manifold of the graph's polygon space. We also connect average-case analysis to a concept known as "generalized hardness," which corresponds to difficulty with respect to a specific geometric structure. Finally, we detail a link between average-case analysis and global minima of the objective landscape for the given problem class.

Formal proof verification systems are capable of confirming the validity of mathematical demonstrations, yet they present such a rigid appearance that their educational application remains limited. De novo genome assembly involves reconstructing an entire, unknown genome from a vast collection of overlapping short DNA fragments, often called reads. Consequently, de novo assembly is an essential component of genomics, enabling the genomic reconstruction of organisms ranging from bacteria to humans. Nevertheless, significant challenges persist for both theoretical computer scientists and biological researchers. Reads may contain errors, and every position within the genome might be influenced by repetitive regions or polymorphisms. Furthermore, existing computer science methodologies still struggle with high memory consumption and inefficient running times. Consequently, our goal is to develop an algorithm capable of assembling genomes with faster execution times and lower resource usage than current leading methods. By leveraging formal language theory—specifically defining an "assembly graph" of a genome as its set of accepted words relative to a set of subwords (reads)—we introduce a new algorithm that computes the genome with the lexicographically smallest name using this graph structure. This formal definition also aids in comparing biological data: reads from an unknown organism can be directly analyzed by examining the corresponding assembly graph of an already known one. Our numerical experiments indicate that a practical implementation of this approach outperforms two current state-of-the-art de novo assemblers in terms of runtime and memory.

For a decade, particle physics has lacked a robust method for performing a grid search for "new physics" without inadvertently overfitting data. We introduce a solution based on machine learning that utilizes "template neural networks" for this scenario. By training these template neural networks on simulated data, we implicitly learn the parameters of potential new physics models. A key advantage is that because the search for new phenomena occurs within the neural network itself rather than the fitted weights, standard overfitting is prevented. We have applied this template technique using a multi-model search within high-luminosity ATLAS data at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis reveals strong local excesses corresponding to strong signal strengths ($>5\sigma$) at $3.0–3.5\,\text{TeV}$ for dileptonic resonant supersymmetry models, although these fluctuations vanish in combination with non-resonant models. All identified local and global significances are non-claim findings. Looking forward, this template machine learning methodology is widely applicable for modeling complex theoretical frameworks.

This study focuses on two core components essential for cross-domain text-to-SQL semantic parsing: 1) extensive surface forms for SQL and 2) high-quality training data sets. To address the former, broad-context language models have demonstrated significant potential in learning contextual representations and improving representation quality. For the latter, current research predominantly relies on domain-specific training data, often struggling with generalization to unseen domains due to a lack of domain-agnostic resources. Consequently, this paper introduces a domain-general training dataset containing large-scale SQL statements across multiple domains. Leveraging a big-context approach with a pre-trained model for enhancing these statements proves particularly beneficial for domains without existing pre-training resources. Furthermore, to further boost cross-domain generalization, a new bucket-level contrastive learning strategy is designed to help the model acquire domain-invariant features. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these contributions.

The ongoing LOFAR Two-metre Sky Survey (LoTSS) seeks to map the Universe's large-scale structure by detecting thousands of galaxy clusters via galaxies within them. The methodology involves estimating the two-point correlation function for these groups using mock datasets. This function determines the probability that a given pair of points—here, representing galaxies—exists. Using partial correlation functions where v_min represents the minimum velocity of a galaxy and v_max the maximum velocity within a bound system, we determined the clustering properties forLoTSS galaxies simulating bound configurations with various mass distributions. Furthermore, we explored the feasibility of distinguishing bound systems from unbounded counterparts by analyzing their correlation functions with a fixed v_min threshold. Finally, we examined how flux calibration uncertainties affect the distinguishability of these populations and the integrity of the calculated two-point correlation function for the bound system.

The high-dimensional rank lasso (HDR LASSO) offers an effective approach for addressing high-dimensional data problems, such as regression and classification, by converting other models into ranks to ensure robustness against outliers in both data values and response variables. Defined as an optimization problem involving piecewise linear and piecewise concave functions segmented by numerous hyperplanes, computing its solution exactly via the standard "grid substitution" method becomes infeasible in high dimensions. This paper introduces an efficient algorithm that overcomes these computational barriers. By exploiting the piecewise structure of the objective function, the authors develop the Multi-Stage Thresholding Algorithm (MSTA), which accurately recovers all grid points. MSTA achieves significant speed improvements over grid substitution. Furthermore, the study establishes the LARS procedure as a precise cold-starting method for initiating MSTA and proves that both strategies retain consistency under specific conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that MSTA outperforms existing solvers such as those found in the **RankLasso** R package and mpppack's **MPM** function in terms of efficiency.

Resolving whether an optimized outcome is local or global has consistently been a major hurdle within optimization theory. In the specific context of minimizing entropy production during the adiabatic relaxation of a quantum many-body chip bathed in a thermal environment from above, we demonstrate the existence of a single, optimal adiabatic pathway using novel methods from large deviation theory. This proof establishes that the objective functional is convex, ensuring global optimality. Notably, this optimization framework accommodates interactions and applies equally to many-body systems with or without them, with the resulting entropy-production-minimizing protocol identified as asymptotically slow. Furthermore, we extend this approach by developing an variational framework capable of locating near-optimal, efficiently realizable protocols for scenarios requiring finite relaxation times. Using this method, we construct approximate optimal strategies for both spin baths and several interacting spin models, detailing the specific dynamics and performance for each.

This paper investigates the intertwined dynamics of opinion alignment and social polarization. We develop a discrete-time model wherein individuals formulate their beliefs in the company of their peers: restricted by a bounded confidence threshold, and influenced exclusively by friends within this circle. While typical research in this area examines polarization at a macro level, our approach focuses on micro mechanisms. We identify specific scenarios under which agents' confidence limits are hereditary across generations, thereby ensuring the preservation of tribal structures. Furthermore, we examine the power configuration within these groups, analyzing how internal influence correlates with an agent's degree of distinctiveness or uniqueness. Ultimately, our investigations reveal that the accumulation of wealth and power follows a Pareto distribution among both tribes, while the aggregate wealth accrued by individual agents also conforms to such distribution at a single-agent scale.

Although genes exhibiting similar transcription activation speeds can produce drastically different mRNA levels over time due to variations in synthesis rates, cell-to-cell variability adds a crucial dimension to this dynamic. This study presents a theoretical analysis of protein production during such phases, examining both mean concentrations and distribution diversity. We demonstrate that although the average level depends on activation rate per gene, two genes with identical activation rates can still maintain diverse variability depending on their specific kinetics, as long as those profiles remain unique. Furthermore, by combining continuous-time models with Markov master equations, we show that both the overall distribution shape and its dependence on activation dynamics increase more significantly in systems governed by distinct polymer mechanisms than in those limited by transcription initiation frequency. These theoretical results were verified through extensive simulations, which also explored the correlation between activation dynamics and the mean-concentration distribution shape. Ultimately, these findings offer a new theoretical basis for simultaneously estimating transcription dynamics, average mRNA levels, and cellular heterogeneity using single-molecule live-cell tracking techniques.

Personalization of Web Search, a significant focus of current web technology, aims to deliver search engine results that are better suited to individual users. This study examines the degree to which personalization affects search diversity and reveals that it frequently leads to relevant information being suppressed, sometimes up to 30%. Furthermore, we introduce the Personalized Measured Deferential Test, a statistical framework designed to evaluate whether the set of relevant links provided by a search engine differs significantly. The analysis also underscores the critical need for incorporating statistical uncertainty when assessing personalization effects, noting that ignoring this factor can result in both false positives and false negatives in the assessment of these impacts.

Program synthesis aims to automatically create software code based on a human's requirements. This paper introduces a framework designed to generate programs using input flowcharts, which serve as precise specifications for control flow and conditionality. We also present a partial differentiability model that analyzes the structural similarity between a candidate program and the target program, acting as a robust heuristic. By integrating this model into a neural search strategy, the system's localization of correct solutions was improved, achieving 58% accuracy on synthetic data derived from flowcharts with an efficiency of 100 per successful synthesis. Although achieving substantial success on challenging real-world datasets resulted in only 23.58% accuracy, the system demonstrated significant boosts through a proposed feedback-loop method for correcting structural bugs. We further release an open API that currently enables the web-based correction of all real-world programs submitted to our platform.

The detection of gravitational waves from neutron star mergers by LIGO and Virgo has provided the first observational confirmation for creating heavy elements through the r-process within these events. We introduce a model for r-process nucleosynthesis tailored to neutron star mergers, accounting for uncertainties in ejecta mass and properties, specifically temperature, entropy, and duration, as measured from light element abundances. Such analyses aim to establish constraints on the astronomical and physical characteristics of the LIGO/Virgo-detected binary neutron star (BNS) merger. For instance, assuming a r-process yield of $\log(A) = 0.95 \pm 0.15$ for K-r-process elements like Krypton suggests BNS ejecta masses ranging from approximately $0.04$ to $0.14\,M_{\odot}$. Consequently, predicting the specific chemical signatures in future cosmic observations requires a deeper comprehension of the hydrodynamics and physics governing these mergers. Furthermore, integrating this research with theoretical nuclear models, nuclear mass models, and nuclear equation of state (EOS) studies can effectively constrain the masses and spins of compact objects involved in the recent LIGO/Virgo BNS detections.
